Determining the uncertainty of machine learning predictions is critical to evaluate their reliability, yet this is affected by various factors, one of which is the degree of model inaccuracy. Since models are inherently simplified representations of reality, model inaccuracy is unavoidable, and this raises concerns about the credibility of estimated uncertainty under such conditions. We contend that model inaccuracy should be given greater consideration, and we illustrate our point with theoretical examples and reference relevant research.

To address the node comparison challenge in integer programming branch-and-bound approaches, a novel siamese graph neural network is proposed. This model represents nodes as bipartite graphs with attributes, and trains an oracle imitator that converges to optimal solutions. The method is evaluated on NP-hard benchmarks where it outperforms a default ranking function in SCIP and other machine learning methods, achieving faster solving times and reduced branch-and-bound trees. The results also hold for larger instances beyond those used for training, and are reproducible using code found at https://github.com/ds4dm/learn2comparenodes.

We investigate multi-agent general-sum Markov games with non-linear approximation capabilities. Focusing on low-rank games, our primary goal is to develop an efficient algorithm that discovers an equilibrium policy without prior knowledge, using both model-based and model-free approaches. These methods utilize representation learning to construct effective models from collected data. Our proposed algorithm achieves a sample efficiency of poly$(H,d,A,1/\varepsilon)$, overcoming limitations in large multi-agent settings by leveraging factorized transition structures. As a notable achievement, our method provides the first efficient algorithm for multi-agent general-sum Markov games with non-linear function approximation.

The Data Bricks Space Mission prototype is a hands-on learning activity that utilizes data physicalization to educate children about data principles. This interactive approach was conceived after researching relevant literature and consulting elementary school educators who specialize in working with 10-12 year olds. By combining Lego bricks with an engaging narrative about a space adventure, teachers can facilitate the Data Bricks Space Mission activity to enable children to generate data, express their insights effectively, and deepen their comprehension of the connection between data and the world.

Predicting the orbits of satellites in low Earth orbit with high accuracy is essential for activities such as conjunction analysis and space situational awareness. This paper examines how uncertainty in atmospheric density estimation affects orbit prediction and proposes methods to mitigate this error. By utilizing machine learning models for density estimation, we investigated the impact of uncertainty on orbit prediction and explored faster methods for propagation. Due to the complexity of atmospheric density correlations, we employed various Monte Carlo methods and the Kalman filtering technique for orbit uncertainty analysis. A more efficient approach was developed by adapting the Kalman filter to account for density uncertainties, allowing for a direct translation of uncertainty. In our validation study, we compared the proposed filter to traditional Monte Carlo methods and proposed an ensemble approach for quantifying orbit uncertainty under different space weather conditions.

Standard conventional cluster-robust standard errors lack robustness, particularly when data consists of a limited number of large clusters. This issue becomes apparent when large clusters significantly outnumber the total sample size, such as in cases like California comprising 10% of the U.S. sample. We demonstrate through formal proof that conventional CR methods are ineffective when cluster sizes adhere to a power law with an exponent less than two. Furthermore, our analysis is supported by recent studies from a top journal, highlighting the shortcomings of CR methods. To address these limitations, we suggest a weighted CR method as a simple, effective solution that has been validated through simulation studies.

The difficulty in using dynamic graphs for prediction arises from extracting specific temporal patterns from a graph that is constantly changing, as well as the issue of having limited and imbalanced task labels for large dynamic graphs. Although recent self-supervised learning advances show promise, they focus primarily on static graphs, while current state-of-the-art models for dynamic graphs are not compatible with self-supervised learning and fail to predict future interactions. To address these challenges, we propose DyG2Vec, a model that can efficiently learn dynamic graph representations using a time-based approach, enabling it to forecast future connections. DyG2Vec outperforms current state-of-the-art models on benchmark datasets while greatly reducing training and inference time. Furthermore, we adapted self-supervised learning evaluation techniques for dynamic graphs, demonstrating that pre-training using this method can produce more stable node representations, especially in scenarios with limited labels.

Gelfand and MacPherson introduced a local and combinatorial formula in 1992 to compute Pontrjagin classes of differential manifolds. Building upon their theory, we expand their original discussion and examine how it established the foundation of combinatorial differential manifolds.

Recent breakthroughs in understanding fission fragment angular momentum have led to a resurgence of interest in this field. Fission physics research heavily relies on concurrent measurements of neutrons and gamma rays in relation to fission fragments. To accomplish this, a sophisticated system was developed, integrating an advanced fission fragment detector with neutron-gamma radiation sensors. A custom-made Frisch-gridded ionization chamber was specifically designed for use with a natural fission source, paired with an array of forty trans-stilbene scintillators. The novel ionization chamber design prioritizes minimal particle loss within its walls, enabling a compact, self-contained system that can be integrated into existing experimental setups. While the ionization chamber measures fission fragment properties, the FS-3 array records neutron and gamma-ray counts and spectra. The setup's component details and preliminary experimental results are presented, along with plans for event-based data analysis and future experiments.

A model of spontaneous scalarization in neutron stars proposed by Damour and Esposito-Farese involves a general relativistic branch becoming unstable and triggering the rapid growth of a scalar field. Applying this concept to cosmology leads to the emergence of a fatal instability in the scalar field during inflation and matter domination, which contradicts solar-system constraints on the field's current value. The introduction of a four-point coupling between the scalar field and an inflaton field by Anson et al., however, revealed that a positive mass squared heavier than the Hubble expansion rate can lead to the suppression of the scalar field during inflation, resulting in a small current value. Our analysis of various inflaton potentials approximated as a quadratic function around the minimum potential value explores the dynamics of the scalar field during reheating and other cosmological epochs in detail. We discovered that within certain ranges of the coupling parameter g, the homogeneous scalar field can be amplified through parametric resonance during coherent oscillations of the inflaton. Our findings indicate that incorporating backreaction of created particles yields maximum values of the scalar field significantly smaller than those without backreaction. Furthermore, we determined that the minimum coupling parameter g consistent with solar-system bounds on the scalar field at the end of reheating is around 10^-5, leaving a wide range of acceptable g values. The scenario proposed by Anson et al. naturally leads to the viable evolution of the scalar field consistent with local gravity constraints without modifying the property of scalarized neutron stars.

Classifying objects from LiDAR 3D point cloud data is vital for advanced applications such as autonomous driving. Nevertheless, annotating these point cloud datasets is extremely time-consuming and demands human annotators to visually inspect the 3D data from various angles. To address this issue, we introduce a semi-supervised learning method that relies solely on pre-existing 3D object models to train robust classifiers that generalize effectively to real-world scenarios. Our approach involves simulating real-world point cloud acquisitions through sampling 3D object models from different viewpoints and incorporating random rotations along with noise to accurately mimic real-world scenarios. These synthesized datasets are then used to train point cloud encoding models such as DGCNN and PointNet++, and their cross-domain classification capabilities are evaluated on real-world datasets. To further advance this field, we create the Point-Syn2Real dataset, a comprehensive benchmark for cross-domain point cloud learning. Our experimental results demonstrate that this novel approach excels over existing methods in terms of cross-domain adaptability in both indoor and outdoor settings.

This paper introduces novel attacks on federated learning when employed to train language-based models. Our research showcases the efficacy of these attacks on a word prediction model within Google's GBoard application, a prominent mobile keyboard app that was one of the first to utilize federated learning in a live production environment. Our results indicate that a user's typed words, such as those used for texting, can be accurately recovered across a broad range of scenarios and that security counter-measures like mini-batching and noise addition are insufficient. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the sequence of words (and consequently, the original sentences typed) can be reconstructed with high precision, highlighting significant privacy concerns due to GBoard's operational status.

In 2019, two bounded Banach space operators were created that are equivalent after extension, but not coupled through Schur, providing an answer to a decades-old question raised by Bart and Tsekanovskii. The constructed operators, being Fredholm operators, have no comparable Banach spaces, and it's known that being Schur coupled implies equivalence after extension for such operators. This paper delves into these two properties for Fredholm operators, not restricted by incomparability conditions on the underlying Banach spaces. The results show that for Schur coupled operators, their index and properties solely rely on the geometry of the Banach spaces, not on the operators themselves. To analyze further, two numerical indices, eae and sc, are defined to capture the relation between equivalence after extension and Schur coupled operators. Examples are provided to demonstrate various values of these indices and their connections to the geometry of Banach spaces, using specific exotic spaces created by Gowers and Maurey and ideas from subsequent works by Aiena, Gonzalez, and Ferenczi.

We've introduced new limitations on the processes governing galaxy formation in extremely distant galaxies by examining a particular, low-mass dwarf galaxy known as Eridanus II, located in the vicinity of our own Milky Way. Using a sophisticated statistical model and analyzing Eridanus II's metal composition, we've found that the galaxy underwent rapid star formation followed by a period of significantly reduced activity. This rapid star formation was accompanied by significant expulsion of newly formed stars and metals. The findings indicate that the majority of Eridanus II's stars were created before the end of the reionization period. The newly established model also predicts how metals and the composition of stars in the galaxy would have changed over time. This research framework can be applied to similar dwarf galaxies in our vicinity to further elucidate the underlying principles governing the evolution of the most faint galaxies in the early universe.

The neutral hydrogen mass function in galaxies at different epochs serves as a crucial indicator of galaxy formation models. Our study of star-forming galaxies at redshifts between 0.20 and 0.42 using radio spectroscopy allowed us to establish the relationship between hydrogen mass and brightness magnitude at redshift 0.35. By combining this relationship with the known luminosity function of star-forming galaxies at these redshifts, we calculated the neutral hydrogen mass function at redshift 0.35 and discovered that accounting for scatter in the relationship was vital. Our findings show that the neutral hydrogen mass function evolved significantly between redshift 0.35 and 0, especially among high-mass galaxies, which have decreased by approximately 3.4 times in prevalence. Conversely, lower-mass galaxies at redshift 0.35 are more abundant than in the local universe. Our study suggests that massive star-forming galaxies acquired hydrogen through mergers or accretion over the past four Gyr.

This article deals with one-dimensional flows that exhibit dispersion and cubic nonlinearities on the real line. Building on recent work, the authors proposed a conjecture that small initial data in the defocusing scenario yield global scattering solutions. This conjecture was proven for a specific type of dispersion relation. Moreover, it was established that the solutions obtained from this proof satisfy certain global bounds and estimates. 

Now, this article examines the focusing scenario, which is potentially more complicated due to the possibility of small solitons. As a result, global scattering solutions cannot be universally expected. However, it is investigated whether the solutions can persist for a long time, and if so, what is the relevant time frame. 

The main contribution of this article, which also applies to the previously mentioned type of dispersion relation, states that for small initial data, the solutions persist for a time scale proportional to $\epsilon^{-8}$. Additionally, on the time scale of $\epsilon^{-6}$, these solutions satisfy certain key estimates and bounds, which is considered a notable achievement given the current state of knowledge.

Thousands of white-light stellar flares have been reported in high-precision observations made by missions such as Kepler, K2, and TESS, which are crucial for assessing biosignatures in exoplanet atmospheres and surface radiation levels around low-mass stars. However, a major limitation in these assessments is the lack of ultraviolet spectrum data on stellar flares. To improve our understanding, we have used simulated data with updated treatment of hydrogen line broadening to predict the ultraviolet flux during a superflare from the star AD Leo. Based on these simulations, we have found that a two-component model can explain the broadening of hydrogen lines, the optical temperature, the Balmer jump strength, and the ultraviolet spectrum shape in the flare's peak phase. By analyzing solar flare data and previous modeling, we have interpreted the two-component model as representing a combination of bright flare kernels and fainter ribbons covering a larger area.

The coupled system we're studying, comprising a physical pendulum and a fluid-filled cavity, is examined under various conditions. We've discovered that the fluid's compressibility plays a significant role in the system's motion. Our findings reveal that the system will eventually come to a rest state, with the fluid's density distribution and the pendulum's equilibrium position being crucial characteristics of this state. We've proven these results using weak solutions and without any specific initial conditions, provided that the system's energy is finite. Additionally, our numerical tests indicate that the system's compressibility, especially when it's high, significantly accelerates its return to equilibrium.
Countable locally standard measure algebras can be parameterized by a Steinitz number paired with a real number that is at least 1.

Recommender systems often struggle with the cold-start issue, especially when a new user joins the platform or a new item is added to the catalog. To tackle item cold-start, our solution replaces the traditional embedding layer in sequential recommenders with a dynamic storage that doesn't require learnable weights and can store a vast number of representations. In this study, we introduce FELRec, a large-scale embedding network that iteratively refines user and item representations as new data becomes available. In contrast to comparable approaches, our model can effectively represent new users and items without requiring additional side information or time-consuming retraining. In item cold-start scenarios, our method surpasses similar approaches by 29.50%-47.45%. Moreover, our proposed model generalizes well across various datasets, even those previously unseen. The accompanying source code is publicly accessible at github.com/kweimann/FELRec.

Modularizing a transducer model for end-to-end speech recognition remains a difficult task, primarily due to the absence of a distinctively separated acoustic model, language model, or blank model. To address this challenge, we introduce the modular hybrid autoregressive transducer (MHAT), which comprises a shared acoustic encoder and two separate decoders for predicting label and blank distributions. MHAT projects the encoder and label decoder outputs directly to acoustic model and internal language model scores before calculating label posteriors. We optimize MHAT through internal language model and HAT losses, thereby allowing its internal language model to function as an independent neural model adaptable to text. Furthermore, MHAT text adaptation leads to significantly improved language model fusion compared to subtraction-based internal language model approaches. On Google's extensive production dataset, a multi-domain MHAT trained on 100 billion sentences yields up to 12.4% relative WER reductions without language model fusion and 21.5% with language model fusion, as compared to 400K-hour trained HAT.

Solutions to complex NP-hard optimization problems have been found by training machine heuristics using sophisticated learning techniques. In particular, classifying graph nodes has been instrumental in identifying an optimal decision boundary to distinguish between nodes in a set and the rest. By applying this approach, a learning framework is used to optimize the graph pruning process, reducing the runtime of maximum clique enumeration. We thoroughly investigate how different node representations affect this method's performance using graph embedding methods such as Node2vec and DeepWalk, and local subgraph feature representations. Our findings indicate that Node2vec and DeepWalk are effective for node representation in classification contexts. Combining local graph features with feature elimination enhances classification accuracy. Lastly, we conduct experiments on random graphs to demonstrate the reliability and scalability of our approach.

This study investigates the transmission of high-frequency waves in highly-scattering environments that exhibit nonlinear absorption effects. Through the employment of advanced mathematical tools like the Wigner transform and multiscale analysis, we establish a class of nonlinear radiative transport equations for the phase-space intensity, as well as their diffusive counterparts. Furthermore, we explore an inverse problem involving the semilinear transport equation, focusing on the recovery of absorption coefficients from a given functional of its solution. Ultimately, we establish a proof of uniqueness for the inverse problem solution.

Melanoma is a skin cancer caused by an abnormal growth of melanocytes, and its treatment through early diagnosis is a critical factor for survival. In order to support this diagnosis through automatic skin lesion segmentation, several Fully Convolutional Network (FCN) approaches have been developed, with the U-Net architecture being particularly effective due to its symmetrical structure. However, the U-Net architecture's reliance on convolutional operations limits its ability to capture long-range dependencies, a crucial factor in accurately segmenting medical images. To address this limitation, a recent innovation has replaced traditional CNN blocks with the Swin Transformer module to capture both local and global representations. This paper proposes a new model, Att-SwinU-Net, which builds on the Transformer-based U-Net architecture by incorporating an attention-based mechanism into the skip connection path to enhance feature reusability. By conducting an extensive ablation study on various skin lesion segmentation datasets, our proposed approach is demonstrated to be highly effective.

Extensive searches under ambient pressure conditions up to 300 GPa were conducted on superhydrides CeBeH$_8$ and CeBH$_8$. Our findings reveal that $Fm\overline{3}m$-CeBeH$_8$ exhibits a superconducting transition temperature $T_{c}$ of 56 K at 10 GPa. Additionally, two more phases with spacegroups $R\overline{3}m$ and $C2/m$ were investigated at increasing pressures, and CeBH$_8$ demonstrates a comparable phase transition process to CeBeH$_8$, though requiring higher pressures and achieving higher $T_c$ values. The predicted phase $Fm\overline{3}m$-CeBH$_8$ is expected to become superconducting above 120 GPa, reaching its maximum $T_{c}$ of 118 K at 150 GPa. Furthermore, $R\overline{3}m$-CeBH$_8$ and $C2/m$-CeBH$_8$ exhibit dynamical stability at pressures above 120 GPa and 100 GPa, respectively. Maximum $T_{c}$ values of 123 K and 115 K are achieved for $R\overline{3}m$-CeBH$_8$ at 195 GPa and $C2/m$-CeBH$_8$ at 350 GPa, respectively. This study adds to the existing knowledge of ternary hydrides and may guide future research in discovering superconducting hydrides at relatively low to moderate pressures.

The movement of biomolecules across a cell membrane is a critical process that underlies the proper functioning of living cells. In this study, we utilize molecular dynamics simulations to model and investigate the transport of polymers through conical channels, exploring the effects of varying pore geometry and polymer lengths on the dynamics of this process. We examine the impact of conical pore geometry and polymer lengths on the total translocation time, waiting time distributions, and velocity profiles of escaping polymer segments. To highlight the asymmetry of the pore, we compare the translocation dynamics from both ends of the conical channel, observing significant differences in agreement with experimental findings. Our investigation also considers the effects of polymer rigidity and increasing chain length on the two types of translocation processes. The study offers insights into the transition from direction-dependent to direction-independent translocation processes through an asymmetric channel.

The objective of precision agriculture is to boost production, minimize workforce expenses, and lower resource consumption through the application of cutting-edge technology in the agricultural sector. Inspired by the bees' visual perception, we have designed an innovative remote sensing system, which integrates UV reflectance into a flower identifier to provide a flower detector. This approach yields detailed images that can be utilized for strawberry flower detection via deep learning algorithms and is applied to an efficient, affordable aerial monitoring robotic system in a scalable manner. Furthermore, we have conducted a comparative analysis of the effectiveness of our UV-G-B image-based detector in comparison to an analogous system utilizing RGB images.

We developed an integrated model by combining the EUropean Heliospheric FORcasting Information Asset (EUHFORIA) and the improved Particle Acceleration and Transport in the Heliosphere (iPATH) model. The integrated model simulated the widespread solar energetic particle event that occurred on November 29, 2020. The simulated SEP event time intensity profiles were compared with observations at Parker Solar Probe (PSP), Solar Terrestrial Relations Observatory (STEREO)-A, Solar and Heliospheric Observatory (SOHO), and Solar Orbiter (SolO). Our study focused on the effects of historical shock acceleration on the varying SEP event time intensity profiles and examined the underlying causes of this widespread event. The simulation revealed that adopting a realistic solar wind background is critical in determining shock expansion and parameters. The simulated SEP event time intensity profiles at PSP showed good agreement with observations, particularly in the presence of an energetic storm particle event. Additionally, the simulated and observed protons time intensity profiles displayed a two-phase enhancement at STA. The findings highlight the significance of using realistic solar wind in modelling shock events to determine SEP event characteristics. The simulation also demonstrated good agreement with observations during the SEP event decay phase at Earth, emphasizing the importance of perpendicular diffusion in widespread SEP events. The integrated model also showed good agreement with SolO observations, suggesting that a possible large curved magnetic field line may be a key factor in understanding the observed SEPs at SolO during the event.

Personalized dose guidance is investigated through Bayesian optimization, which identifies the optimal drug dosage suited to each individual's needs, ultimately enhancing therapeutic results. The use of the interior point method in the learning process ensures high patient safety. This concept is exemplified by optimizing bolus insulin doses for patients with type 1 diabetes, addressing the effects of meal consumption. The proposed algorithm, requiring no initial information about the patients, effectively improves the therapeutic outcome while maintaining safety standards. Additionally, other potential applications of this method in healthcare are examined.

Deep learning techniques have become prevalent in processing point cloud data across various scientific fields. However, models based on geometric deep learning are typically complex and difficult to interpret, posing significant challenges in scientific research and experimentation. This study introduces a novel framework called learnable randomness injection, allowing the development of inherently interpretable models based on general geometric deep learning backbones. Once trained, models induced by this framework can pinpoint specific points in point cloud data that hold crucial information related to prediction labels. To validate the proposed mechanism, we created four real-world scientific datasets spanning high-energy physics and biochemistry domains. In comparison to existing post-hoc interpretation methods, LRI-induced models demonstrate significantly better and more stable alignments with meaningful scientific patterns. The proposed framework is grounded in the information bottleneck principle, and models developed through this framework exhibit improved robustness in the face of training and testing distribution shifts. The code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/Graph-COM/LRI.

This paper introduces the Value Iteration Network for Reward Shaping (VIN-RS), a reward shaping mechanism leveraging a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). By integrating a CNN trained on data from a Hidden Markov Model, VIN-RS generates predicted shaping values from environmental images or graphs. Building upon recent limitations in reward shaping regarding Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) and transition matrices, VIN-RS effectively constructs a potential function and automatically infers the transition matrix. This is achieved through a self-learned convolution filter and environmental detail extraction from input frames or sampled graphs. Utilizing the success of message passing in reward shaping and CNN planning behavior, VIN-RS is trained using these messages. We evaluate VIN-RS on various games, including tabular games, Atari 2600, and MuJoCo, with promising results in learning speed and cumulative reward improvement over the state-of-the-art.

Segerman's 15+4 puzzle offers a hinged twist on the traditional 15-puzzle where tiles rotate upon movement. A 1974 Wilson classification of sliding block puzzles is expanded upon here to include rotating tiles, where solutions form subgroups of the generalized symmetric groups. It is observed that in all but two specific instances, a puzzle's solution set will either comprise the entire generalized symmetric group or a subgroup of index two, specifically one of two unique subgroups.
In this paper, we disprove certain hypotheses made by Marques and Lengyel regarding the p-adic values of terms within the Tribonacci sequence.

Deep learning technologies, particularly Graph Optimal Transport-based particle tracking, have significantly improved the understanding of three-dimensional turbulent flows found in both natural phenomena and industrial processes. However, traditional particle tracking methods still face challenges related to accurately tracking particles with large displacements and high-density distributions, while minimizing computational costs. To address these challenges, a novel deep neural network called GotFlow3D was developed to learn 3D fluid flow motion from double-frame particle sets using an end-to-end approach. GotFlow3D constructs two graphs that capture both spatial and feature-based information, thereby enriching particle representations with intrinsic and extrinsic features. These features are then utilized to create optimal transport plans that establish particle pair correspondences, guiding iterative and adaptive recurrent flow learning. Experimental evaluations demonstrate GotFlow3D's state-of-the-art performance in particle tracking and scene flow learning, boasting exceptional accuracy, robustness, and generalization capabilities that provide profound insights into complex physical and biological systems.

Exceptional points, a type of spectral degeneracy found in optics, acoustics, and other non-conservative systems, are at the center of many fascinating phenomena. Although researchers have studied these points extensively over the past two decades, they still don't fully understand the collective behaviors that occur when multiple exceptional points or lines interact with each other. We have identified a universal non-Abelian conservation rule that applies to these interactions in multiband non-Hermitian systems and have discovered several unexpected behaviors. Our findings show that two exceptional points with opposite charges don't always annihilate, and the rules we've uncovered impose constraints on the possible arrangements of exceptional lines. We've shown that certain patterns, like the Hopf link, are impossible, but others, like staggered rings made of non-commutative lines, are possible. Our results have the potential to be implemented in platforms like acoustic cavities, optical waveguides, and ring resonators and will help researchers develop a deeper understanding of exceptional non-Abelian topology and the various ways it can be manipulated.

Electrical distribution network faults pose significant risks, including fires and electrocution. High current Low Impedance Faults are relatively easy to identify and mitigate. Conversely, High Impedance Faults, which are equally hazardous, present a detection challenge due to lower fault currents and complex time-varying behavior. This issue is particularly pertinent in New Zealand's extensive and mostly unmonitored distribution networks. 

We have established a physical testing facility for analyzing power system faults and have been developing a sensing and fault detection system. By simulating both Low and High Impedance Faults, we characterized their distinct behaviors in 400V networks and created a deep learning-based classifier to identify the type of fault present. A pole-mountable sensor system has been designed and installed in Wellington Electricity's network for ongoing testing and evaluation.

This paper will outline our test facility and the experience of developing the sensing system. Notably, the most varied High Impedance Fault behaviors observed were in experiments involving a tree branch, so the paper will primarily focus on those results. Other surface material fault results will be reported separately. Additionally, the paper will discuss the installed pole-mountable sensor system and its current performance outcomes.

Optimizing the transport of ore from mines to ports is a major concern in mining supply chains due to escalating costs and resource scarcity. Major mining companies are seeking the most efficient way to allocate their resources to minimize operational expenses. Researchers have previously explored this issue as a resource-constrained job scheduling (RCJS) problem, and various optimization methods have been proposed for the deterministic version. However, the inevitable uncertainty in resource availability in mining operations has received limited attention. Solving RCJS with uncertainty is a complex optimization problem that existing methods cannot efficiently address. To address this limitation, a novel adaptive population-based simulated annealing algorithm is introduced, capable of overcoming existing methods' shortcomings, including premature convergence, excessive hyper-parameters, and inefficient uncertainty handling. This algorithm effectively balances exploration and exploitation through a population-based approach, adaptive cooling schedule modification, and a mechanism to select perturbation operators dynamically. Experimental results demonstrate the proposed algorithm's superiority across various RCJS benchmark instances and uncertainty levels, achieving new best-known solutions for all but one problem instance.

A fundamental concern in contemporary physics revolves around verifying the presence of a quantum or classical nature of gravity in a controlled laboratory setting. To assess this question, researchers have proposed an experiment where two close neutral masses are put into a superposition state to observe the entanglement brought about by the quantum nature of gravity, yet with sufficient separation to minimize the impact of other known Standard Model interactions. However, creating these superposition states for a lighter mass necessitates the presence of a heavy system, typically a piece of laboratory equipment, that can induce gravitational decoherence. To examine this issue further, we will analyze pairs of probe-detector systems, consisting of two light and two heavy oscillators, to determine under what conditions entanglement between the two light systems can persist despite being influenced by the heavy systems, culminating in a prediction for the degree of decoherence expected in the proposed experiment designed to investigate the quantum aspects of gravity.

By extending the scope of language technologies to encompass diverse languages and modalities, researchers have created numerous opportunities for NLP tasks. However, much of the related research has focused on a single language, namely English, or a single text modality. To break this mold, researchers have initiated an interdisciplinary investigation into integrating multimodal and multilingual streams, known as MultiX. A primary aim of this research is to create a comprehensive overview of existing work by categorizing various tasks, datasets, and methods for addressing complex MultiX scenarios. To this end, we will provide a detailed examination of languages studied, annotated data, and how different languages and modalities interact in modeling processes. Subsequently, we will analyze the strengths and weaknesses of various modeling approaches and present the dominant trends within the field. Finally, we will conclude by outlining potential challenges and promising avenues for future research.

A significant merger is occurring in the Milky Way, with the Sagittarius dwarf galaxy being torn apart as it orbits our galaxy. The resulting close passes disrupt the Milky Way's disk, and through simulations, researchers have investigated how massive satellite galaxies on a similar orbit affect the star formation within our galaxy. The study confirms that satellite interactions enhance star formation in the host galaxy but finds that gas-poor satellites produce brief, intense star formation bursts during close passes. Conversely, gas-rich satellites result in a more prolonged star formation increase without significant bursts. The stripping of gas from satellites smooths out variations in star formation. The satellite's impact mainly affects the outer parts of the galaxy, and close passes contribute to the formation of low-metallicity stars within our galaxy. The research supports a link between the recent Sgr galaxy passes and a burst of star formation in the solar neighborhood but indicates that an even closer pass was required to replicate an earlier burst of star formation.

The interplay between antiferromagnetism and chiral-d wave superconductivity in a honeycomb lattice, near an antiferromagnetic state at half band filling, is explored using the t-J model and a slave boson mean field theory. The study examines the order parameters and single particle dispersion relations across various band filling fractions, revealing that antiferromagnetism boosts superconductivity, leading to nodal dispersion relations at two distinct band fillings. The emergence of these nodal dispersion relations, contrary to expectations, is discussed. Furthermore, the characteristics of chiral-d wave superconducting states are compared to those of AF extended-s wave states, shedding light on the notable features of chiral-d wave superconductors. This research has implications for materials such as the In$_3$Cu$_2$VO$_9$ compound with a honeycomb lattice structure.

High-resolution neutron imaging is a complex process that requires precise detection techniques. Achieving micrometer-scale resolution in neutron imaging is crucial, but developing suitable detectors is a significant challenge. Nuclear emulsion-based neutron detectors offer a potential solution due to their fine grain structure. To enhance image quality, a high track density is necessary; however, current analysis methods struggle to handle such high densities. Simulated data were utilized to determine the optimal track density for neutron imaging applications. It was found that a density of approximately 10,000 tracks per square micrometer is sufficient for high-resolution imaging. The study also explored contrast resolution in images with varying track densities and neutron transmission rates. Experiments were conducted using neutron-imaged gadolinium-based gratings with well-known geometries, resulting in successful grating structure resolution. The edge response was calculated to be around 0.945 micrometers, with a 4 nanometer margin of error.

For 6G cellular networks, Joint Communication and Sensing (JCAS) is crucial, balancing fast wireless connectivity with sensing the environment, particularly human presence. To anticipate signal blockages, recognizing blockages first requires sensing, and we test this with human motion detection as a simpler task. Our experiments using both qualitative visual inspections and quantitative DL model analysis validate using a smaller human motion dataset from a 26 GHz device with hybrid beamforming to pre-train or test DL models. The DFS data collected is then used to verify hypotheses. Our findings indicate that (i) domain shift affects DL model performance, (ii) diluting DFS data may be counterproductive, (iii) insufficient data leads to poor inference results, (iv) lower sensitivity can be addressed by increasing activities per frame and lowering the sampling rate, and (v) optimizing sampling rates may enhance performance but needs to be assessed case-by-case.

A common challenge in numerous real-world scenarios, such as marketing campaigns, loan management, and e-commerce, is identifying the optimal match between items and their respective owners. These assignment problems can be formulated as complex optimization tasks, but they often fall under the category of NP-hard problems, making them difficult to solve when the number of items or owners is substantial. In this paper, we aim to tackle large-scale assignment problems, with millions of items and tens of owners, by relaxing the constraints and reformulating the optimization problem. The objective function is now convex, and the constraints are linear or convex and separable, making it easier to solve. We propose using the Bregman Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (BADMM) framework to break down the problem into smaller subtasks, which can be solved in parallel using a distributed computation framework. Our approach is tested on both simulated and real-world datasets to demonstrate its accuracy and efficiency.

We've developed a new method of wireless image transmission using deep joint source-channel coding (DeepJSCC) for multi-input multi-output (MIMO) Rayleigh fading channels. The receiver only has access to channel state information, so we're employing two different transmission strategies: one leveraging spatial diversity and the other utilizing spatial multiplexing. In the diversity method, we're using orthogonal space-time block codes to ensure full diversity and enhance the resilience of transmission against channel fluctuations. In contrast, the multiplexing approach enables users to directly map the code to antennas, with additional degrees of freedom used to convey more information about the source signal. Simulation results demonstrate that the diversity scheme performs better at lower signal-to-noise ratios and fewer receive antennas, but becomes less effective when the number of transmit antennas exceeds two. Additionally, we've found that both diversity and multiplexing schemes can match the performance of state-of-the-art BPG algorithms at MIMO capacity under the considered scenarios.

A novel algorithm called replica exchange preconditioned Langevin diffusion discretized by the Crank-Nicolson scheme (repCNLD) is presented to tackle high-dimensional and multi-modal distribution problems. The task of sampling from such distributions is particularly challenging. Standard Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods often degrade as parameter dimensions increase and struggle to capture all modes in non-convex energy landscapes. The repCNLD approach, however, improves the convergence rate of the single-chain preconditioned CN Langevin diffusion and enables it to identify all modes within the distributions. Furthermore, the algorithm utilizes a robust Crank-Nicolson discretization that ensures linear growth of the discretization error in relation to the chosen time step size. The repCNLD is also adapted for multi-variance settings to accelerate convergence and reduce computational requirements. Moreover, an unbiased estimator of the swapping rate is derived for the multi-variance repCNLD, which serves as a guide for the selection of the low-fidelity model in the second chain. The effectiveness of the method is demonstrated through the application of high-dimensional Gaussian mixture models and high-dimensional nonlinear partial differential equation (PDE) inverse problems, where the discrete adjoint method is leveraged to efficiently compute gradients for the latter.

A common method used to analyze large whole-slide images (WSIs) from annotated WSIs is Multiple Instance Learning (MIL). In MIL-based pipelines, WSIs are typically split into sections and feature maps created to decrease computational costs and memory usage when training. To address this limitation, we propose the EmbAugmenter, a network that generates data augmentations in a compressed form rather than directly on the images, leading to substantial speed improvements. Our experiments with the SICAPv2 dataset reveal that EmbAugmenter outperforms traditional MIL without augmentation and rivals the effectiveness of patch-level augmentation while requiring significantly less time.

This summary presents an update on the current research into CP violation and mixing in B-meson decays. Through analysis of the $B^0_d \to J/\psi K^0_S$ and $B^0_s \to J/\psi \phi$ decay processes, the study concentrates on accurately determining the mixing phases $\phi_d$ and $\phi_s$, taking into consideration uncertainties resulting from hadronic interactions using available data. However, the observed patterns of CP violation in the non-leptonic decays of $B$ to $\pi K$ and $B^0_s$ to $D_s^{\mp} K^{\pm}$ are inconsistent and raise intriguing questions. Could these anomalies potentially be evidence of new physics phenomena?

We explore efficient techniques for retrieving specific derangements and ménage permutations from a lexicographically ordered list, effectively unranking them. Given a list in lexicographic order, we aim to develop an algorithm that can efficiently extract the k-th permutation from it. Our approach involves reducing this problem to a counting problem where we calculate the number of restricted permutations starting with a given prefix, and then apply rook theory to solve it. This research has potential applications in various fields, including combinatorics, probability, statistics, and modeling.

Graph Neural Networks are enhanced Neural Networks that utilize a graph's structural relationships to improve performance. Although GNNs are thought to excel in many applications, they can sometimes offer limited or even worse performance than conventional Neural Networks that are unaware of the graph structure. To pinpoint these instances, we introduce two new metrics that draw from graph signal processing and statistical analysis. These metrics enable us to determine when the use of graph relationships provides a performance advantage. Based on the results, we can establish a threshold to predict whether graph-aware models will outperform their graph-agnostic counterparts.

Our proposed character-level white-box adversarial attack method targets transformer models by leveraging the fact that words are divided into subtokens before model input. The method's core lies in three steps: first, a gradient-based approach identifies the most susceptible words in a sentence; second, these words are segmented into subtokens to replace the original tokenization outcome; third, an adversarial loss guides the substitution of replaceable subtokens using the Gumbel-softmax trick to enable gradient backpropagation. To minimize character alterations, we incorporate visual and length constraints during optimization. Experimental results on sentence-level and token-level tasks reveal that our approach surpasses prior attack methods in terms of success rate and edit distance, and human evaluations confirm that our adversarial examples retain their original labels.

The remnants of supernovae and their interaction with the interstellar medium play a crucial role in influencing the environment. The warm molecular hydrogen in these areas typically assumes the responsibility of cooling down the shocked molecular gas, a process which has been observed in the form of near-infrared emission lines. Recent studies have, however, been hindered by limitations in filter imaging and mid-infrared spectroscopic observations with relatively poor angular resolutions. This paper discusses near-infrared spectroscopic mosaic observations taken towards specific areas of the supernova remnant IC 443, utilizing the K-band Multi-Object Spectrograph (KMOS) on the Very Large Telescope. The obtained data reveal 20 H2 ro-vibrational transitions, one H line, and two Fe II lines, dominating broadband images at both H- and K-bands. The spatial distribution of H2 lines across different areas shows clumpy structures on various scales, ranging from approximately 0.1 pc down to approximately 0.008 pc. The calculated excitation temperature of H2 ranges from 1500 K to 2500 K, indicating the presence of warm gas in these regions. The comparison of multiple gas phases within the areas indicates stratified shock structures across all regions. This supports the existence of multiple types of shocks within the same areas. The spectroscopic data obtained also verifies previously identified candidates for young stellar objects in these areas, with the result that none of them are associated with young stars. This discovery poses challenges to the previously proposed scenario of star formation being triggered by supernova remnant shocks in IC 443.

To accelerate neural network training and minimize energy consumption, data quantization is an effective strategy. However, traditional methods of quantization often result in reduced accuracy or limited bit-width compression. Current methods that combine different levels of precision are capable of high compression but struggle with assigning optimal bit widths. Our approach introduces DYNASTY, a novel method of training neural networks that dynamically adjusts precision on a block-by-block basis. This framework uses real-time analysis to determine data sensitivity and adaptively assigns bit widths to maintain training stability. Our experimental results demonstrate that DYNASTY achieves a $5.1$ times increase in speed and a $4.7$ times reduction in energy consumption compared to an 8-bit baseline, all while preserving accuracy and incurring minimal hardware overhead, when tested on challenging datasets such as CIFAR-100 and ImageNet.

The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) is being explored to showcase quantum advantage on near-term computers, but device errors prevent reliable execution for larger problems. In QAOA, a problem's graph translates to a circuit where edges correspond to two 2-qubit CNOT operations. Due to CNOT's error-proneness, QAOA circuit fidelity correlates with the number of edges. Observing that real-world application graphs follow a "power-law" distribution with hotspot nodes, we propose "FrozenQubits", which freezes these nodes and partitions the state-space into smaller sub-spaces, making corresponding QAOA sub-circuits more resilient to errors. In contrast to prior approaches, FrozenQubits doesn't require post-processing. Evaluations with 5,300 circuits on eight IBM quantum computers demonstrate that FrozenQubits improves solution quality by an average of 8.73x, with up to 57x improvement, at the cost of 2x more resources.

Explaining the dynamic behavior of matter has led some to consider the role of natural laws, geometric structure, or the spacetime manifold. Nevertheless, certain approaches, like those that appeal to the geometric structure or the spacetime manifold itself, are considered overly metaphysical by some. Conversely, other scholars propose reversing the explanation process, focusing on dynamics as the primary aspect to consider. This perspective has been implemented in theories such as Best Systems Analysis (BSA) and Regularity Relationism. These theories treat natural laws as codifications of dynamic patterns in matter and the geometric structure as representations of these patterns as well. This thesis contributes a new perspective of the spacetime manifold as merely a codification of dynamic patterns in matter. It develops advanced mathematical tools to analyze various spacetime settings within the context of multiple spacetime theories, thereby initiating a competition between different codifications of spacetime analogous to the one between different law-like codifications. This competition will be evaluated based on how well these codifications align with the theory's dynamics and kinematics rather than on simplicity and strength.

BLI with minimal bilingual guidance is an essential yet intricate task in multilingual NLP. Current top BLI techniques rely on generating cross-lingual word representations to identify cross-lingual word similarities. To achieve this, existing methods typically use static models, extract type-level representations from pre-trained language models, or combine these approaches. Our proposed semi-supervised post-processing reranking method, BLICEr, can enhance the BLI capabilities of any pre-calculated cross-lingual representation space. By extracting lexical knowledge from pre-trained language models and combining it with existing representations, we improve BLI performance. To accomplish this, we create a word similarity dataset, fine-tune a cross-encoder model to predict similarity scores, and combine its output with the original representation scores at inference time. Our novel approach achieves new state-of-the-art results on various BLI benchmarks and robustly outperforms strong baselines across multiple languages, and demonstrates its flexibility with diverse cross-lingual representation spaces.

Images and labels for rare disease diagnosis are difficult to come by, due to the limited number of affected patients and the expertise required for annotation. The skewed distribution of certain disease classifications further hampers progress. Traditional training methods often fail due to biased class priors. Few-shot learning approaches aim to address these issues, but they require adaptation to low-data regimes. This study focuses on enhancing meta-learning for dermatological image classification. A proposed baseline approach utilizes a network to generate transferable feature representations that can be applied across various few-shot tasks. Our method aligns with previous research suggesting that straightforward feature representations can be more effective than complex meta-learning methods. The efficacy of this proposed method is demonstrated through experiments on dermoscopic images, showing that simple linear classifiers trained on these representations can outperform traditional meta-learning approaches.

Niobium is an extensively researched superconductor due to its significant applications and exceptional properties. It boasts the highest superconducting critical temperature at 9.33 K among all pure metals, contributing to its importance in alloy-based power applications, as well as sensitive magneto-sensing, radio-frequency cavities, and superconducting qubits. To optimize the performance of these devices, understanding the electronic and superconducting characteristics of niobium, particularly its normal and superconducting anisotropies, is crucial for preventing quantum coherence loss. Recent theoretical models describe the anisotropic features of niobium in the presence of disorder, prompting an experimental investigation into the effect of disorder caused by 3.5 MeV proton irradiation of thin Nb films, similar to those used in transmon qubits. Through measurements of the superconducting critical temperature and upper critical fields, we demonstrate a notable decrease in $T_c$ resulting from potential, non-magnetic scattering, which directly relates to the anisotropic order parameter, showing a remarkable quantitative agreement between theoretical predictions and experimental results.

Public art installations in urban areas can profoundly affect individuals' feelings of belonging and perceived cultural representation. A new study presents a graph-based method, incorporating localized limitations, to develop an interactive platform for art curation that fosters diverse and inclusive public spaces. Building on Schelling's theory of segregation, the study constructs a matrix of costs to guide the selection process, using projected gradient descent to determine the optimal placement of artwork. By integrating fairness measures and minimum representation criteria, the algorithm minimizes biased "in-group" preferences in art allocation, while also evaluating its potential drawbacks and limitations through a case study at Tufts University.

The interplay between quantum mechanics and gravity has significant implications in various phenomena, including the origins of the Universe and Hawking radiation, but our knowledge is limited due to the absence of experiments that allow us to study these effects in a controlled and observable manner. We propose a novel experimental approach using a superposition state photon passing through two rotating Sagnac interferometers with distinct diameters, representing a superposition of different spacetimes. Our simulations demonstrate the potential for genuine entanglement generation, even at low rotation speeds, and suggest that Earth's rotation can facilitate these effects. This setup provides an accessible platform to investigate how spacetime influences the emergence of entanglement.

We examine the non-perturbative implications of a Mathieu differential equation deformation compatible with $\mathcal{PT}$ symmetry, starting with a reparameterization that establishes a connection between non-Hermitian and Hermitian scenarios in the complex plane. By restricting the $\mathcal{PT}$ deformation parameter, we ensure the preservation of $\mathcal{PT}$ symmetry information within the Hermitian context, a factor present throughout non-perturbative outcomes and in the transseries representation of the deformed Mathieu partition function. In quantum mechanics, the $\mathcal{PT}$ symmetry parameter influences the real instanton solution for the deformed Mathieu potential within the Hermitian framework, causing it to become smoother as its value increases, modifying the instanton width due to a decrease in the potential barrier height. This effect is observed in both single-instanton and multi-instanton configurations as well as in the bounce limit of instanton-anti-instanton pairs whose dynamics can be likened to the resistively shunted junction (RSJ) model.

Over the past few years, there has been growing concern about air pollution globally, particularly in countries of the northern hemisphere, where large-scale air quality monitoring systems are being implemented to inform decision-making. However, these initiatives have some significant limitations: (1) they come with a hefty price tag and are often difficult to set up quickly; (2) their focus on urban areas may perpetuate existing inequalities; and (3) the air pollution estimation process lacks clarity. In this study, we propose a cost-effective solution to estimate air pollution using publicly available data on road structures, with a focus on England and Wales in the UK, although our method can be applied to other regions. Our approach enables policymakers to make informed decisions based on accurate air pollution estimates, covering not just urban areas, but all districts, and with a transparent and explainable process. We demonstrate that a linear regression model utilizing a single structural property, such as the length of road networks within districts, can pinpoint the most polluted areas in England and Wales to within 0.36% accuracy. Our model presents a low-cost, yet effective, alternative to existing models, making it an attractive option for policymakers seeking to implement clean-air initiatives without significant investment. Its practical application, accessible design, and global dataset coverage also make it suitable for low-income countries seeking to establish air pollution estimation systems.

Currently, end-users lack access to substantial amounts of Adaptive-Optics (AO) control loop data and telemetry. Expanding accessibility to this data could significantly impact the AO landscape by addressing various use cases, including PSF derivation, turbulence analysis, and control optimization. To overcome a significant barrier to data sharing, the lack of standardization, we introduce an object-oriented Python package for AO telemetry. This package's data model separates users from the underlying FITS-based standard, enabling compatibility with diverse existing and future AO systems, both raw and abstracted from specific instrument details. We demonstrate the package's utility with data from active AO systems on 10-meter-class observatories, currently supporting AOF and Keck, with further expansions planned.

This is the third paper in a series focusing on creating virtual structure sheaves and $K$-theoretic invariants in moduli theory. Almost perfect obstruction theories, developed by Y.-H. Kiem and the author, are the primary subjects of study to define $K$-theory invariants for various moduli stacks, including those for generalized $K$-theoretic Donaldson-Thomas invariants. 

In this work, we prove virtual Riemann-Roch theorems in almost perfect obstruction theory contexts, both non-equivariant and equivariant, with an extension to cosection localized versions. This expands on the previous work of Fantechi-Göttsche and Ravi-Sreedhar by removing technical requirements. Our key technical contributions include treating the equivariant $K$-theory and Gysin map for sheaf stacks, as well as a formula for the virtual Todd class.

In the field of neuroscience, researchers traditionally test hypotheses through the analysis of neuropsychological and behavioral data to identify relationships between specific life events and health outcomes, such as depression. However, recent advancements in deep learning offer a promising alternative to these traditional methods by enabling the prediction of outcomes from a wide range of contributing factors. Despite its potential, this approach has faced limitations as the significance of the findings was not adequately tied to the evidence supporting the underlying hypotheses. To address this issue, our study proposes a novel method that combines the principles of permutation testing with the capabilities of deep learning to facilitate the integration of hypothesis-driven testing into the analysis of complex data. We apply this method to data collected from a large-scale adolescent study, the NCANDA, which consists of self-reported assessments of over 600 participants. Using our approach, we are able to successfully identify distinct categories of risk factors that contribute to the manifestation of major depressive disorder symptoms.

This article aims to investigate the Lp-boundedness of pseudo-differential operators on a homogeneous tree structure. It is proven that for 1 < p < 2, the Lp-boundedness of these operators on the tree can be linked to their counterparts on the group of integers. Additionally, an equivalent of the Calderon-Vaillancourt theorem is demonstrated for the case of a homogeneous tree, specifically for 1 < p < infinity excluding 2.

We introduce a fairness metric that deviates from the conventional equal odds fairness paradigm for classification by removing the need for complete equality. Our approach involves an iterative, adaptable, and model-agnostic grid-based strategy that adjusts outcome predictions for each sensitive attribute value to align with the proposed fairness measure. This strategy is designed to effectively manage attribute values with multiple possibilities and ensures a per-attribute cleansing of outcomes across different protected attribute values. Furthermore, we have expanded our strategy to accommodate multiple attributes. Through an illustration of its application in fraud detection, we demonstrate that our proposed strategy achieves fairness across various values of a single protected attribute as well as multiple protected attributes. In comparison to current fairness methods, which primarily focus on two groups, our strategy achieves comparable performance on several publicly available datasets.

This paper showcases a practical version of the Diverting Fast Radix (DFR) Algorithm, known as ThielSort, and compares its performance to existing algorithms in its field. By outlining theoretical improvements and providing detailed implementation specifics, the paper demonstrates ThielSort's competitive edge.

To investigate whether entropy is conserved between Big Bang nucleosynthesis and recombination, we examine the hypothetical decay of a massive particle into photons and other relativistic species, using Planck temperature and polarization data, COBE/FIRAS spectral distortion constraints, and primordial deuterium abundance measurements to limit these decay scenarios. When between $56\%$ and $71\%$ of the particle's energy is transferred to photons, the number of effective particles during recombination remains mostly unchanged, allowing for significant entropy injection according to Planck data alone. The inclusion of spectral distortion bounds restricts the decay rate of the massive particle to be greater than $1.91\times10^{-6} \text{s}^{-1}$ at a $95\%$ confidence level. We discover that bounds on the energy density of the massive particle are significantly strengthened by the inclusion of constraints on the primordial deuterium abundance, allowing the particle to contribute no more than $2.35\%$ ($95\%$ confidence level) of the universe's total energy density before it decays.

We investigate Edgeworth expansions in the context of limit theorems for self-normalized sums, specifically developing non-uniform bounds for these expansions under minimal moment conditions. This includes a novel extension to cases involving non-integer moments and reduced remainder. Furthermore, we establish non-uniform bounds for local limit theorems, which in turn enable the derivation of refined expansions in the entropic central limit theorem and total variation distance for self-normalized sums.

Researchers working in the field of quantum thermodynamics aim to fully understand the application of thermodynamic principles in extremely quantum systems. Despite significant advancements, creating machines where quantum effects play a crucial role remains challenging. In a recent study, the researchers conducted an experiment measuring the actual impact of quantum mechanics on a fundamental thermodynamic relationship. By utilizing a single trapped ion, they successfully simulated thermal equilibrium and quantum interactions to test the quantum version of this relationship. The results from the experiment align with the theoretical quantum version of this relationship and contradict the classical version with a high level of confidence. Furthermore, the study rules out the possibility of measurement errors as an explanation for the results and shows that the quantum correction is only present at low temperatures.

This study explores minimal supersymmetric AdS$_3$ solutions in type IIA and IIB supergravity on $G_2$-orientifolds using the bispinor formalism. A conclusive argument is established that AdS$_3$ solutions are not possible in massless type IIA string theory on such $G_2$-backgrounds. In contrast, some AdS$_3$ solutions in massive type IIA supergravity do exhibit a scale separation, whereas this is not the case for type IIB vacua. A 3d superpotential formula in the bispinor language is derived for both type IIA and IIB configurations. The supersymmetry conditions of this superpotential are shown to reduce to the bispinor equations.

In our lecture series, we'll cover the probability laws governing random points, curves, and surfaces. Starting with a review of key concepts including martingales, one-dimensional Brownian motion, and the $D$-dimensional Bessel processes, we'll delve into Dyson's Brownian motion model, which is an extension of the latter. We'll then use the reproducing kernels of Hilbert spaces to introduce Gaussian analytic functions and determinantal point processes, which arise from the zeros of these functions. Next, we'll explore the Schramm-Loewner evolution, a complex-valued process that generates conformally invariant probability laws for random curves in the upper half complex plane. We'll view this process as a complex extension of the Bessel processes, with specific parameter relationships. Finally, we'll construct multiple SLE$_{\kappa}$ processes, which are driven by interacting random processes on the real line and produce multiple, interacting random curves in the upper half complex plane. We'll demonstrate that a specific coupling between multiple SLE and the Gaussian free field is established when the driving process is related to Dyson's Brownian motion model.

We analyze a general model of gravity that involves a single scalar, examining how the gravitational degrees of freedom influence inflation. The effects of massive spin-2 particles on inflation are considerable, enabling the spontaneous breakdown of global scale invariance without requiring additional scalar fields. The calculations of inflationary parameters are compared to existing models and found to be consistent with the constraints imposed by Planck and BICEP/Keck data on inflation.

This research aims to develop an approach for generating synthetic sequential data within the Synthetic Data Vault framework. To accomplish this, we have created a new model based on an existing Sequential model in SDV. This model utilizes an end-to-end framework that generates a multi-sequence generative model for real-world data. We introduce a novel machine learning model, the Conditional Probabilistic Auto-Regressive model. The entire system and its accompanying models are available in the open-source Synthetic Data Vault library. Following the development of the Sequential SDV, we employed it to generate synthetic data and compared its performance to a CTGAN-based model. We devised a new metric, the Multi-Sequence Aggregate Similarity, to evaluate the synthetic data. Our results show that the sequential SDV model captures more complex patterns without compromising synthetic data quality.

Utilizing maximum-likelihood estimation to determine experimentally measurable values
that can constrain models is crucial in many physics experiments. A Profiled Feldman-Cousins method,
described in detail, addresses common issues in constructing precise confidence intervals:
insufficient data, constrained parameters, and the need for proper handling of extraneous variables.
This method provides superior frequentist coverage compared to other techniques in use, and is
broadly applicable to parameter estimation in neutrino oscillation studies and analogous measurements.
We detail the implementation of this method within the framework of the NOvA experiment.

The paper investigates minimum energy issues in the presence of external forces on a locally compact space $X$ using a function kernel $\kappa$ that adheres to the principles of energy and consistency. It identifies sufficient and necessary conditions for the existence of a minimum measure $\lambda_{A,f}$ that minimizes the total energy, defined by two integral equations, over all positive measures concentrated on a given subset $A$ of $X$. These conditions address a long-standing question in the field. The findings are specifically applied to a class of kernels, such as $|x-y|^{\alpha-n}$, where $\alpha$ and $n$ are specific parameters. The study provides alternative characterizations of the minimizing measure $\lambda_{A,f}$ and explores its continuity properties under certain conditions. The obtained results have significant implications for various kernels in classical and modern potential theory, offering novel insights and understanding of the underlying phenomena.

In the field of computer vision, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have been
leading the way due to their capability to extract relevant features and excel
in classification tasks, such as analyzing medical images like X-rays. Although
these algorithms are highly effective, their complexity as black-box models
makes it difficult to comprehend the decision-making process behind them.
To overcome this challenge, researchers employ eXplainable AI techniques to
evaluate their applicability in various fields. In medical imaging, classification
problems are often binary or multiclass, but real-world scenarios often involve
multiple co-occurring symptoms, such as in chest X-rays, which necessitates the
use of multilabel classification models. However, these models can be affected by
class imbalance, where some labels have significantly fewer instances than others.
This paper contributes to the field by developing a novel deep learning approach
for handling imbalanced, multilabel chest X-ray datasets. It sets a baseline for
the underutilized PadChest dataset and proposes an innovative eXplainable AI
methodology based on heatmaps, which includes probabilistic outputs and
inter-model comparisons. Our results show promise, especially considering the
high number of labels involved. Notably, the heatmaps accurately identify areas
of interest, aligning with the expected regions that human experts would focus
on to make informed decisions.

Within the framework of gravothermal evolution of a monatomic fluid, I investigate the dynamic instability of a fluid sphere in (N+1) dimensions by applying Chandrasekhar's criterion to quasistatic equilibria along the evolutionary sequence. Upon triggering instability, it is likely that the fluid would collapse into a black hole unless halted by another interaction. The dimensionality of (3+1) spacetime is unique as it is the critical dimension at which the fluid is stable yet not overly so, and it allows stable hydrostatic equilibrium even with a positive cosmological constant. Higher-dimensional (N>3) spheres are inherently unstable, while (2+1) spacetime is too stable according to both Newton's and Einstein's theories. The role of a negative cosmological constant is vital for the Banados-Teitelboim-Zanelli (BTZ) black hole solution and the equilibrium configurations of a fluid disk, and this supports the cosmic censorship conjecture as there is no unstable configuration for a homogeneous fluid disk to form a naked singularity. However, BTZ holes with mass can emerge from collapsing fluid disks. The implications of spacetime dimensionality are discussed briefly.

A widely studied method of phase imaging called ptychography has led to non-invasive nanoscale imaging and various applications in material science and defense industries. However, one significant limitation of ptychography is the lengthy data collection time due to the requirement for substantial overlap between adjacent illumination areas. Typically, approaches with reduced overlap yield reconstructions with imperfections, while traditional methods cannot achieve satisfactory results without significant overlap. This paper proposes an innovative method that combines sparse, acquired data with data generated by a pre-trained deep generative network to meet the oversampling requirement in ptychography. Consequently, this hybrid approach can significantly shorten the experimental data collection time. To validate the proposed method, we compare the reconstruction quality to existing approaches and discuss the advantages and disadvantages of this new technique.

Maximizing the Gini index can lead to flawed decisions due to its inherent limitations, specifically that it doesn't produce a strictly consistent scoring rule. The primary concern arises from the Gini index's nature as a rank-based metric that's not sensitive to calibration issues. Nonetheless, by focusing on auto-calibrated regression models, we find that the Gini index can indeed produce strictly consistent scoring.

For countably infinite tensegrities, asymptotic equilibrium stresses are defined. This leads to generalizations of the first-order rigidity characterization by Roth-Whiteley, as well as rigidity concepts for infinite bar-joint frameworks, including second-order rigidity and prestress stability. These concepts provide sufficient conditions for continuous rigidity in certain bounded motions, based on a newly established proof that prestress stability guarantees continuous rigidity in finite frameworks.

This paper introduces Language Models as Data (LAD), a new approach for generating diverse and accurate synthetic data to aid in zero-shot task-oriented dialog. By incorporating GPT-3 to foster linguistic diversity, LAD enables the training of downstream neural dialog models that meet necessary structural requirements. Experimental results demonstrate notable performance improvements in zero-shot scenarios, with +15% intent prediction accuracy, +31.4 F-1 score for slot filling, and +11 F1 for next action prediction. Moreover, interactive human evaluations suggest that training with LAD yields comparable outcomes to training with real human dialogs. The LAD framework has been made publicly available, along with its code and data, at https://github.com/Shikib/lad.

Consider a primitive character $\chi$ modulo a prime number $q$ and a positive real number $\delta$. The large order of $\chi$ has previously been shown to have an analogous relationship to Vinogradov's conjecture on quadratic non-residues. Specifically, it was found that if the order of $\chi$ is sufficiently large, namely greater than or equal to $d_0(\delta)$, then $\chi(n)$ is not equal to 1 for some positive integer $n$ less than or equal to $q^{\delta}$. We provide a new and simpler proof of this result. Additionally, it is proven that when the order of $\chi$ is square-free, for any $d$th root of unity $\alpha$, the number of integers $n$ less than or equal to $x$ such that $\chi(n)$ is equal to $\alpha$ is negligible compared to $x$ for any $x$ greater than $q^{\delta}$. Consequently, for $\chi$ of sufficiently large order, the values of $\{\chi(n)\}$ cannot cluster around 1 for any $\delta > 0$. The proof of this result relies on a non-trivial second moment estimate for short sums of the characters $\chi^\ell$ averaged over $1 \leq \ell \leq d-1$ when $d$ has no small prime factors. Specifically, it is shown that for any $\delta > 0$, for almost all powers $1 \leq \ell \leq d-1$, the partial sums of $\chi^\ell$ exhibit cancellation in intervals $n \leq q^{\delta}$ when $d$ is sufficiently large, which extends the work of Burgess. Our argument combines results from pretentious number theory and additive combinatorics. Finally, it is proven that the Pólya-Vinogradov inequality may be uniformly improved for $\chi^\ell$ averaged over $1 \leq \ell \leq d-1$ for prime $3 \leq d \leq q-1$, extending the work of Granville and Soundararajan.

Developing AI systems capable of lifelong learning is a significant challenge, and various methods and assessment tools have been suggested to analyze algorithmic characteristics. Nonetheless, existing metrics for evaluating lifelong learning are often distorted by task and scenario complexity. To address this issue, we present an explainable model-free approach to estimate key attributes of lifelong learning algorithms. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through experiments using simulated data. Additionally, we validate the structural integrity of our model by examining real-world performance data from well-known lifelong learning methods and baseline models applied to lifelong classification and lifelong reinforcement learning scenarios.

In the realms of science and technology, optical imaging is extensively utilized across various industries and academic institutions. A key aspect of image sensing involves analyzing a digitized image to obtain measurements such as an object's position.
